impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's prior-art date analysis under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2) must require a written description analysis of a provisional application under Dynamic Drinkware, or whether the Board's Penumbra framework—requiring only ministerial requirements and description of the relied-upon subject matter—governs under the AIA.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's final written decision finding Dental Monitoring's patent claims unpatentable as obvious, and remanded for further consideration of whether a prior art reference (Carrier) was entitled to its provisional application filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court addressed the critical question of what standard applies to determine a reference patent's effective prior art date when relying on a provisional application under the AIA. This decision has significant implications for inter partes review proceedings and the scope of prior art available to patent challengers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether prior art references can claim earlier provisional filing dates, potentially narrowing the universe of prior art available to IPR petitioners and strengthening patent validity defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty establishing prior art dates based on provisional applications, potentially increasing the cost and uncertainty of patent challenges.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for method claims directed to administering a genus of antibodies for treating headache requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claimed genus, or whether enablement of the treatment limitation is sufficient.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of its panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation, contrary to Supreme Court enablement precedent. Multiple amici including major pharmaceutical companies supported rehearing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method claims, particularly in the biopharmaceutical space, benefit from a more permissive enablement standard that may allow broader genus claims to survive validity challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the pharmaceutical and biotech industries face potentially broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, which may increase licensing costs and limit freedom to operate with alternative antibodies in the same genus.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining the university. The court also held that the licensee had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to enforcement activities. This decision clarifies important questions about standing for exclusive licensees and the scope of rights transfer necessary to maintain patent infringement suits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities, benefit from clearer standards confirming their ability to enforce licensed patents independently without joining the patent owner, reducing procedural obstacles to enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense of challenging standing based on the licensee's business model or the completeness of the license agreement's rights transfer.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of Federal Claims properly assessed copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation rather than deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement, and what constitutes permissible use of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in calculating government copyright infringement damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation to assess damages for the government's infringement of copyrighted software (TETRA®) rather than deferring to an existing license agreement. However, the court vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The decision provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government procurement contexts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders gain clarity that courts may use hypothetical negotiation frameworks to calculate infringement damages even when existing license agreements are available, potentially yielding higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The government and large-scale software licensees face the risk that copyright damages may exceed the rates established in actual license agreements, and the limits on the 'book of wisdom' doctrine may complicate damages calculations.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's six-year statute of limitations for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings claims arising from the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc., which distinguished between equitable tolling rules and statutory filing deadlines.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from a firm limitations period in the Court of Federal Claims, providing certainty about when potential liability from past actions expires without risk of tolling from class action filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims cannot rely on the pendency of a class action to toll the statute of limitations, meaning they must independently file claims within the six-year window or risk permanent forfeiture of their rights.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied judgment as a matter of law of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents related to non-uniform constellation technology used in digital communication systems, while affirming eligibility of the '509 and '922 patent claims. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL of non-infringement and the admission of damages expert testimony. This decision refines the § 101 eligibility analysis for technology standards patents and has significant implications for patent holders in the telecommunications sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards benefit from clearer boundaries on patent eligibility, and the affirmance of damages methodology provides guidance for future patent litigation involving standards-essential technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting broad claims related to mathematical or algorithmic innovations in communications standards face renewed scrutiny under § 101, potentially requiring remand and additional proceedings to establish eligibility.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on dissimilarity rather than substantial similarity, and whether functional claim construction issues in design patents should be decided by juries rather than judges.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent infringement case, with a concurrence defending the Egyptian Goddess framework and a dissent from Chief Judge Moore (joined by Judge Reyna) arguing the framework improperly changed the infringement inquiry to focus on differences rather than similarity, enabling courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without proper jury consideration. Judges Stoll and Stark also dissented without opinion. This case highlights a significant intra-circuit split on design patent infringement standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the current framework that permits courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment when designs are sufficiently distinct, potentially reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face risk that the current Egyptian Goddess framework may allow courts to dismiss infringement claims at summary judgment based on differences without adequate consideration of overall similarity or prior art, undermining design patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's clause regarding whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, or whether such a dispute is a state law contract interpretation issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute between T-Mobile and KAIFI regarding the meaning of 'survives the EPR' in a patent litigation settlement agreement, because the dispute was fundamentally one of state law contract interpretation that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies negotiating patent settlements gain clarity that disputes over settlement agreement interpretation will typically be resolved in regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially providing more predictable outcomes based on established contract principles.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements may face uncertainty about which court will hear post-settlement disputes, and the transfer to regional circuits may result in less patent-specialized review of agreements with patent-related terminology.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of VDPP's patent infringement complaint without leave to amend and the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, finding the case exceptional. The court also addressed sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The decision reinforces that courts may deny leave to amend when the proposed amended complaint is futile and may award fees in meritless patent cases, particularly where the plaintiff implicitly agreed not to amend as part of an extension agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the affirmance of fee awards in exceptional cases, deterring meritless patent infringement suits and providing a mechanism to recover defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial risk when pursuing infringement claims that courts deem meritless, including joint and several liability for attorney fees and sanctions.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue and patent eligibility grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the same order, after first finding venue improper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a patent infringement case on both improper venue and § 101 eligibility grounds in a single order. The plaintiff argued the court should not have addressed eligibility after concluding venue was improper, but the Federal Circuit held the district court did not err by also ruling on eligibility. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was found ineligible for patenting under § 101.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain dispositive rulings on multiple grounds simultaneously, potentially precluding re-filing of claims in a proper venue and reducing the risk of prolonged litigation over ineligible patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders, particularly those with business method patents, face the risk of having claims adjudicated on the merits even in an improper venue, which could preclude them from re-asserting the same patents elsewhere.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims of a patent directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler using a transformer with a non-magnetic core are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), despite surviving an indefiniteness challenge.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed final judgment of invalidity of the asserted claims of the '385 patent, but on enablement grounds rather than the district court's indefiniteness rationale. The court reversed the indefiniteness finding but agreed with Samsung's alternative argument that the claims failed the enablement requirement. This decision demonstrates that appellate courts will reach alternative invalidity grounds to affirm judgments and highlights the independent nature of enablement and indefiniteness inquiries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple paths to invalidate overly broad or poorly supported patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that even if their claims survive one invalidity challenge, appellate courts may affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not addressed by the trial court, requiring robust support for all validity requirements.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which imposes no express deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews within 15 days of notice of initiation is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The court found the statute silent on timing and held the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This decision preserves Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping sunset reviews and protects domestic manufacturers' ability to maintain antidumping orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers and producers benefit from the preservation of Commerce's regulatory framework for sunset reviews, which supports the maintenance of antidumping duty orders protecting against unfair foreign competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face continued enforcement of Commerce's procedural deadlines that may result in the continuation of antidumping duties, with limited grounds to challenge the regulatory framework.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court's denial of Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 must include sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorney fees in a patent case where the patentee had filed suit despite prior § 101 rejections of related patent claims by the PTO post-Alice. The court held the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful review of whether the case was exceptional under § 285 or whether sanctions were warranted. This decision emphasizes courts' obligation to explain their reasoning when denying fee motions in potentially exceptional patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers seeking fee-shifting in meritless patent cases benefit from the requirement that courts provide detailed reasoning when denying sanctions motions, increasing accountability for patentees who file questionable suits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk that fee denials will be vacated and reconsidered on remand, particularly when patents have a history of § 101 rejections in related applications.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's determination that certain debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean government-owned creditor conferred no countervailable benefit on a steel manufacturer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and reinstated Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions performed by Dongbu Steel conferred countervailable benefits warranting countervailing duties. The court held that the trial court erred in sustaining Commerce's later determination, made under protest after remands, that the conversions conferred no benefit. This decision reinforces the framework for evaluating government equity infusions and their treatment under U.S. countervailing duty law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from the reinstatement of countervailing duty determinations that protect against subsidized foreign competition through government-directed financial restructuring.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers receiving government financial support through debt-to-equity conversions face increased risk of countervailing duties, even when later Commerce determinations found no benefit, as courts may reinstate original adverse findings.
